{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=preference+formation+memory+dependent+decisions+path+dependence+longitudinal+behavior+active+learning&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7355192\", \"title\": [\"Associative Memory, Path-Dependent Beliefs, and Asset PricingDynamics: A Deep Learning Approach\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Do historical market crashes continue to depress asset prices long after fundamental recovery? This paper develops a continuous-time general equilibrium model where investors&apos; growth expectations are driven by associative memory retrieval. Because belief formation depends on the infinite-dimensional history of returns and volatility, the valuation equation yields a path-dependent partial differential equation. I solve this system using a causal LSTM-based Deep BSDE solver validated against an exact analytic benchmark to five decimal places. Empirically, I construct a strictly backward-looking Memory Resonance Index (MRI) that identifies crash anchors using only historical price paths. In China&apos;s retail-dominated CSI 300 index (2005--2025), a one-standard-deviation increase in daily MRI predicts a 0.21 percentage point decrease in next-day excess returns (t=-4.71). The effect survives flexible controls for nonlinear momentum and volatility, and a 500-draw random-anchor placebo test confirms that the crash-detection algorithm is essential (p<0.002). In the U.S. S&P 500, however, MRI has no incremental predictive power and is spanned by VIX and valuation ratios. The model rationalises this contrast: associative memory generates significant contemporaneous valuation discounts in price levels, while market frictions and limits to arbitrage dictate whether these cognitive distortions translate into predictable return dynamics.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7355192\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"title\": [\"Public Transit Path Choice Modeling with Behavior Driven Preference Learning: An Interpretable Framework\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Public transit path choice behavior modeling is fundamental to travel demand analysis and transit guidance strategies. Discrete choice models based on Multinomial Logit remain the dominant approach for path choice analysis, yet predictive accuracy is frequently constrained by underlying assumptions; conversely, the few exiting deep learning-based methods suffer from weak interpretability. More importantly, neither method effectively captures individual preferences, making it difficult to reflect traveler heterogeneity. To address these limitations, a behavior-driven preference learning-based public transit path choice model is proposed in this study. First, individual behavioral features are constructed using historical data, and a preference mining layer is designed to learn latent preference representations from long-term historical behaviors. Then, gating mechanisms and attention mechanisms are introduced to achieve differentiated attention to path features among different travelers. Furthermore, a comprehensive model interpretation framework is developed by leveraging methods such as Accumulated Local Effects, Integrated Gradients, and Adaptive Clustering. Finally, empirical studies are conducted based on real-world data from Beijing, and comparative analyses with existing methods are performed. Performance analysis results indicate that an accuracy rate of 83.90% is achieved by the proposed model, representing a improvement of 11.86 percentage points. Furthermore, it is demonstrated through interpretability analyses that complex nonlinear relationships among intricate path features, contextual features, and individual preferences can be more effectively captured. Additionally, the distinctly different decision-making logics exhibited by various preference groups during the path choice process are reasonably explained.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7331065\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1006/game.1996.0032\", \"title\": [\"Path Dependence and Learning from Neighbors\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0032\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1996, 4]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1016/j.procir.2021.05.067\", \"title\": [\"Active preference learning in product design decisions\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procir.2021.05.067\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2021]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "f0cdb7212bbe6548ae3f8034ed8ec502a3f16d312ad40f41a4963f95111eca87", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "emergent_preferences", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7355192", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7331065", "doi:10.1006/game.1996.0032", "doi:10.1016/j.procir.2021.05.067"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7355192", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7331065", "https://doi.org/10.1006/game.1996.0032", "https://doi.org/10.1016/j.procir.2021.05.067"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
